name: Online Schema Migrations
intent: Change a table's structure while the application keeps running, by splitting the change into small compatible steps instead of one big blocking ALTER.
scenario: A users table with 100 million rows has one full_name column. The product needs first_name and last_name. Traffic is about 2,000 writes per second and must not stop, and read replicas (extra copies that serve reads) must not fall minutes behind.
problem: A schema change that rewrites or locks a large table blocks writes for as long as it runs: minutes to hours on 100 million rows. Writers queue behind the lock, connection pools fill, and the outage looks like the database died. Even without a table lock, one giant UPDATE holds row locks and one huge transaction, produces a replication event the replicas cannot apply for a long time, and cannot be rolled back cheaply. Meanwhile the application is deployed gradually, so old and new code run against the same table at the same time.

howItWorks.title: Expand: add the new shape without breaking the old one
howItWorks.text: ADD COLUMN first_name and last_name as nullable with no default. In PostgreSQL this is a catalog change, in MySQL 8 it can be ALGORITHM=INSTANT. The lock is taken for milliseconds, but it still queues behind any long running transaction and blocks everyone behind it, so set lock_timeout (or retry) and run it at a quiet moment. Old code ignores the new columns and keeps working.

howItWorks.title: Dual-write before backfill
howItWorks.text: Deploy an app version that writes full_name and first_name/last_name together, in the same statement, while still reading full_name. This must be live everywhere before the backfill starts. Otherwise a row written after the backfill has passed it keeps a stale split, and nothing will ever repair it.

howItWorks.title: Backfill (fill the new columns for existing rows) in small, throttled batches
howItWorks.text: A job walks the primary key in ranges of a few thousand rows: UPDATE users SET first_name = ..., last_name = ... WHERE id BETWEEN a AND b AND first_name IS NULL. Each batch is a short transaction (hundreds of milliseconds), so row locks are brief and the WAL or binlog (the log of changes that replicas replay) is produced in small pieces. Between batches it sleeps while replica lag (how far a replica is behind the primary) is above a threshold, so replicas and any lag-sensitive reads are not sacrificed. The WHERE first_name IS NULL guard means the job never overwrites a value the application wrote moments ago.

howItWorks.title: Verify, switch reads, stop writing the old column
howItWorks.text: Count rows where the new columns are NULL or differ from the split of full_name, and wait until replicas have caught up. Then flip reads to the new columns behind a flag. Keep dual-writing for a while so you can flip back. When confident, deploy the version that no longer touches full_name.

howItWorks.title: Contract: drop the old column
howItWorks.text: DROP COLUMN full_name once no deployed code, job, report or replica consumer references it. In PostgreSQL this is metadata only; in MySQL it can rewrite the table, so use INSTANT where available or a shadow-table tool. Each step is its own deploy and can be reverted on its own.

howItWorks.title: Shadow-table tools for changes that must rewrite the table
howItWorks.text: gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change create an empty copy with the new schema, copy rows in chunks (INSERT IGNORE ... SELECT), and capture ongoing changes (gh-ost reads the binlog, pt-osc uses triggers) to replay on the copy. When the copy has caught up, a short atomic rename swaps the tables. They throttle on replica lag, but they cannot compute a column from other columns. Splitting full_name still needs a backfill, which is why the expand and contract pattern is the usual answer here.

pros: No long table lock: the only blocking moments are millisecond metadata changes and, for shadow tools, a rename of around a second
Every step is small, observable and reversible, and old and new app versions can run at the same time
Backfill speed is a dial: it can be slowed or paused when replicas lag or the primary is busy
Works for data transformations that no ALTER TABLE can express, such as splitting or merging columns
cons: Takes days or weeks of calendar time and several deploys instead of one command
Temporarily doubles the writes for the changed columns and uses extra storage and WAL or binlog volume
Dual-write code is extra code that must be written correctly and then removed
Shadow-table tools need disk space for a full copy, extra care with foreign keys and triggers, and do not fit every topology (some managed services restrict them)
whenToUse: Large or hot tables where an hour of blocked writes, or minutes of replica lag, is not acceptable
Changes that must keep the old and new application versions working during a rolling deploy
Data transformations (split, merge, re-encode, change type) rather than a plain metadata change
whenNotToUse: Small tables, or a service with a maintenance window, where a plain ALTER finishes in seconds and the ceremony costs more than the risk
Changes the database already does online and cheaply: PostgreSQL ADD COLUMN with a constant default, MySQL 8 INSTANT operations, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
Pre-launch tables with no traffic and no data worth preserving
pitfalls: Starting the backfill before dual-write is live everywhere: rows written behind the cursor keep a stale split silently

A backfill that reads a row, computes in the app, and writes it back unconditionally: it overwrites a concurrent update with stale data. Compute in SQL, in one statement, and guard with IS NULL or a version

ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... NOT NULL DEFAULT on an old engine, or with a volatile default, rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock. Adding NOT NULL later takes a full scan under lock unless you first add a validated CHECK constraint (PostgreSQL) and then set NOT NULL
CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY (PostgreSQL) blocks all writes for the duration of the build; CONCURRENTLY is slower, cannot run inside a transaction, and leaves an INVALID index if it fails
Renaming a column or changing its type in one step breaks every running app instance that still uses the old name or type. Add a new column and migrate instead
Waiting for a metadata lock behind a long transaction: the ALTER queues, every later query queues behind the ALTER, and the whole table stalls. Always set lock_timeout and retry
Ignoring replica lag: finishing the backfill on the primary does not mean replicas have the data. Switching reads to the new columns while a replica is 20 minutes behind returns NULL names
One huge batch because it is faster: the batch holds locks for seconds, produces a single large replication event, and a failure rolls back all the work

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Old and new app versions, deployed gradually, that read and write the table throughout the migration.

roles.label: Users table
roles.description: The 100 million row table on the primary, which gains new columns and eventually loses the old one.

roles.label: Backfill job
roles.description: Copies data into the new columns in small batches and sleeps when replicas lag.

roles.label: Read replica
roles.description: Applies the primary's changes in order and falls behind if the migration produces too many too fast.

quiz.question: A team splits users.full_name into first_name and last_name on a table with 2,000 writes per second. They add the nullable columns, run a backfill over the whole table, and only then deploy app code that writes all three columns together. What goes wrong?
options: Old app versions crash because they find columns they do not know about
The backfill holds a table lock until the new code is deployed, so writes queue up behind it
Rows changed behind the backfill cursor keep a stale split that nothing repairs
Replicas cannot apply the backfill, so reads return NULL names for weeks
quiz.explanation: Dual-write must be live everywhere before the backfill starts. Otherwise a row changed behind the backfill cursor has a new full_name and an old split, and the IS NULL guard never revisits it. Old code simply ignores extra nullable columns, and a backfill does not need to wait for replicas to apply anything.

quiz.question: On a 100-million-row PostgreSQL table, a team runs ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN first_name text, a metadata-only change, at peak traffic. A 10-minute analytics transaction is already reading the table. What happens?
options: The ALTER waits for its lock and later queries queue behind it, stalling the table
It finishes in a few milliseconds because adding a nullable column only changes the catalog
It rewrites all 100 million rows under an exclusive lock for the full duration
It fails at once with an error because another transaction is using the table
quiz.explanation: The change itself is instant, but it needs a brief exclusive lock, and it cannot get it until the analytics transaction ends. Every later query then queues behind the waiting ALTER. Setting lock_timeout and retrying avoids the stall.

quiz.question: A backfill job reads 5,000 users per batch, splits full_name in application code and writes the result back with UPDATE users SET first_name = ?, last_name = ? WHERE id = ?. Dual-write is live, and customers keep renaming themselves. Some users end up with a split that does not match their new name. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the batch size to 500,000 rows so the job finishes before many names change
Compute the split in SQL in a single UPDATE and add WHERE first_name IS NULL
Run the whole backfill in one transaction so it works from a single snapshot
Compute the split on a replica and copy the results to the primary
quiz.explanation: Reading, computing in the app and writing back unconditionally can overwrite a newer value with stale data. A single statement guarded by IS NULL never touches a row the application already wrote. Bigger batches and one huge transaction only hold locks longer and widen the race, and a replica cannot write the results to the primary.
